Editors have highlighted the following attributes while ensuring the content's credibility: fact-checked trusted source proofread The GIST Add to Preferred Sources Credit: Unsplash/CC0 Public Domain With El Niño winter storms rolling in, coastal communities will naturally brace for the obvious: surging high tides, pounding waves and seawater spilling over seawalls. Decades of storm coverage have encouraged us to measure climate risk by what crashes onto the shoreline. But this hyperfocus on the surface misses the real threat already unfolding beneath our feet. Now, UC Berkeley researchers are uncovering how rising water tables threaten coastal cities long before the ocean overtakes the beach—and how we can redesign our communities to live with higher water. In this 101 in 101 video, part of our series in which a Berkeley expert explains an aspect of their work in 101 seconds, Berkeley environmental planner Kristina Hill shares a pivotal factor that is redefining climate adaptation: rising groundwater. Hill, a professor in the Department of Landscape Architecture & Environmental Planning, uses spatial modeling and hydrological data to map how sea level rise affects urban infrastructure. Coastal cities are built into a dry crust of land supported by a layer of fresh groundwater, which floats like a pillow over dense saltwater pushing from the ocean into the land. As ocean levels rise, that subterranean saltwater wedge presses farther inland, driving the fresh groundwater toward the surface. Since the water pressure comes from below, conventional barriers like levees or concrete seawalls are eventually bypassed. Hill's research demonstrates that rising groundwater causes issues long before surface seawater reaches the front door. It backs up sewer pipes, corrodes building foundations and—most concerning to Hill—mobilizes buried toxins and soil contaminants. Regional water table mapping across coastal environments is central to this research. By analyzing thousands of groundwater measurements across the San Francisco Bay Area and beyond, Hill's team has mapped thousands of legacy industrial sites , from old military facilities to chemical plants, that sit directly in the path of rising groundwater. Working alongside community organizers and municipal leaders, Hill and her colleagues are transforming how climate resilience is evaluated on the ground. The team's groundwater models reveal a striking environmental justice implication: Low-income neighborhoods and communities of color disproportionately bear the burden of living near these vulnerable, contaminated zones. Reframing the issue this way shows that groundwater rise, and therefore sea level rise, are active public health emergencies, rather than a distant shoreline concern. Instead of trying to wall out the ocean or abandoning coastal neighborhoods, Hill emphasizes adaptive engineering strategies that embrace rising water. Drawing inspiration from historical innovations like Tenochtitlan's ancient floating districts in what is now Mexico City, as well as modern Dutch water engineering, her work highlights floating housing built on new, excavated water bodies, Japanese superdikes and restored wetland habitats. Combined with field monitoring and public engagement, these design approaches show that cities can protect public health, preserve property values and maintain social ties by learning to live with higher water. Shifting the conversation away from fighting the sea toward adaptations that teach coastal communities to live with higher water gives a practical blueprint for resilience, Hill said. Addressing the threat from below empowers cities to innovate, build smarter and thrive in a changing climate.
